# Audio Understanding Beyond Words {#sec-paralinguistics}

Every chapter so far has treated audio as a carrier of words. Recognition
extracts them, synthesis produces them, codecs compress the signal that contains
them, and speech language models reason about them. This chapter is about
everything else in the signal.

That residue divides into two families. **Paralinguistic** attributes are
properties of the speaker and the delivery rather than the message: emotion,
age, accent, health, arousal, whether the utterance is sincere. **Non-speech
audio** is the rest of the acoustic world: a door closing, a siren, rain, a
violin. They are conventionally separate research communities with separate
venues, and this chapter treats them together because they share a difficulty
that the tasks in earlier chapters do not have.

That difficulty is the label. Word error rate works because a transcript has a
correct answer, and disagreement between annotators is rare and resolvable. Ask
two people whether a speaker sounds angry or merely emphatic, or to describe a
five-second recording in a sentence, and they will disagree — not through
carelessness, but because the question does not have a single answer. Almost
everything distinctive about this area follows from that.

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading order

This chapter assumes @sec-ssl (encoders and layer-wise specialisation) and
touches @sec-slm-tasks, which noted that these tasks are increasingly posed as
prompts to an audio language model. That framing is where the field is going;
this chapter is about what it is absorbing, and about the measurement problems
it inherits in doing so.
:::


## The Annotation Problem {#sec-label-problem}

Consider what a "ground truth" emotion label is. An annotator listens to an
utterance and selects a category. A second annotator hears the same utterance and
selects a different one. Neither is wrong. The label that reaches the dataset is
usually the majority vote, which discards the disagreement and presents the
result as though it were fact.

Three consequences follow, and they recur through every section below.

**Reported accuracy is bounded by human agreement**, which for categorical
emotion is frequently in the range of 0.3–0.6 by chance-corrected measures such
as Krippendorff's $\alpha$. A model reporting 75% accuracy against majority-vote
labels on a corpus where annotators agree 60% of the time is reporting something
other than what the number appears to say.

**The majority vote is a lossy summary of a distribution.** A clip where seven of
ten annotators say *angry* and three say *frustrated* is genuinely different from
one where ten of ten say *angry*, and collapsing both to `angry` throws away the
distinction. **Soft labels** — training against the annotator distribution with a
cross-entropy or divergence objective rather than a one-hot target — are the
standard response, and are now common practice in emotion and sound-event work
alike.

**Evaluation must respect the same fact.** Scoring a prediction against one
reference when many are valid is the same structural problem as MOS in synthesis
(@sec-mos) and as the one-to-many problem in generation (@sec-onetomany). It is
the reason audio captioning needed its own metrics rather than borrowing image
captioning's, as @sec-aac describes.


## Audio Classification Backbones {#sec-audio-backbones}

The non-speech side of the field was organised by one dataset. **AudioSet**
[@gemmeke2017audioset] is roughly two million ten-second YouTube clips labelled
against an ontology of 527 sound classes, and it played the role for audio that
ImageNet played for vision: large enough that pre-training on it transfers, and
standard enough that everyone reports on it.

| Model | Idea | Why it mattered |
|:------|:-----|:----------------|
| **PANNs** [@kong2020panns] | Large CNNs (notably CNN14) trained on AudioSet, released as transferable feature extractors | Established AudioSet pre-training as the default starting point for audio tagging |
| **AST** [@gong2021ast] | Treat the spectrogram as an image; a pure ViT [@dosovitskiy2021vit] over patches, **initialised from ImageNet weights** | Removed convolutions entirely; the cross-modal weight transfer is the surprising part |
| **SSAST** [@gong2022ssast] | Self-supervised AST pre-training by masked patch prediction | Removed the dependence on AudioSet labels |
| **BEATs** [@chen2023beats] | Iterative pre-training that alternates between learning an **acoustic tokeniser** and a masked-prediction model over its discrete labels | Brought HuBERT's iterative refinement (@sec-hubert) to general audio; the standard general-audio encoder, and SALMONN's non-speech branch |

: Backbones for general audio classification. {#tbl-audio-backbones}

Two observations are worth drawing out. AST's initialisation from ImageNet
weights works despite a spectrogram not being an image in any meaningful sense —
its axes are time and frequency, not two spatial dimensions, and translation
invariance along frequency is *wrong* for audio, since shifting a harmonic stack
upward changes the sound. That it transfers anyway says something about how
generic early ViT features are.

And BEATs closes a loop this book has traced twice. It is HuBERT's insight —
that the quality of a masked-prediction target can be improved by re-deriving it
from the model you just trained — applied to general audio rather than speech
(@sec-hubert). The same idea reappears in codecs as semantic distillation
(@sec-semantic-acoustic).


## Weak Labels and Temporal Localisation {#sec-weak-labels}

AudioSet labels are **clip-level**: a ten-second clip is marked as containing a
dog bark, with no indication of when. **Sound event detection** requires the
onset and offset. This is a mismatch between the supervision available and the
output required, and it is the technical core of the non-speech side.

The standard formulation is **multiple-instance learning**. The model produces a
frame-level probability $y_t$ for each class and pools it to a clip-level
prediction compared against the weak label. Max pooling is degenerate — it
propagates gradient to one frame — and mean pooling dilutes short events, so the
usual choice is **attention pooling**, in which the model learns its own
weighting:

$$
\hat{y} = \frac{\sum_{t} y_t \, w_t}{\sum_{t} w_t},
\qquad w_t = \sigma\big(\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_t\big)
$$ {#eq-mil-pool}

The frame-level $y_t$ is never directly supervised; it emerges as the byproduct
of explaining a clip-level label. That is an elegant trick and also a fragile
one, since nothing forces $y_t$ to be temporally accurate as long as the pooled
value is right.

The DCASE challenge's long-running Task 4 formalised the harder realistic
setting: a small strongly-labelled set, a larger weakly-labelled set, and a large
unlabelled set. The standard method is **mean teacher** [@tarvainen2017meanteacher]
— an exponential moving average of the student's weights supplies consistency
targets on unlabelled audio — imported directly from semi-supervised image
classification, and structurally the same EMA-teacher device that data2vec uses
for representation learning (@sec-data2vec).

Evaluation has its own subtlety. Event-based F-score with a fixed tolerance
("collar") around each boundary depends heavily on an arbitrary collar width and
on a chosen operating threshold. The **polyphonic sound detection score**
[@bilen2020psds] replaces both with a threshold-independent, collar-free
formulation that integrates performance across operating points and explicitly
separates confusion between classes from missed detections. It is now the
standard DCASE metric, and the reasoning behind it — that a metric which moves
when you change an arbitrary hyperparameter is measuring the hyperparameter —
generalises well beyond this task.


## Speech Emotion Recognition {#sec-ser}

Emotion is represented in two incompatible ways, and much confusion in this
literature comes from comparing across them.

**Categorical** representations assign a discrete label from a small set
(angry, happy, sad, neutral). They are intuitive and align with how people talk
about emotion, but the categories are culturally specific and the boundaries are
not sharp. **Dimensional** representations place an utterance in a continuous
space, conventionally **valence** (pleasant–unpleasant), **arousal**
(calm–excited), and sometimes **dominance**. They avoid forcing discrete choices
and are the more defensible target, and they are scored with the **concordance
correlation coefficient**, which rewards agreement in both correlation and
absolute scale:

$$
\rho_c = \frac{2\,\rho\,\sigma_x \sigma_y}{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + (\mu_x - \mu_y)^2}
$$ {#eq-ccc}

Categorical work reports weighted and **unweighted** accuracy, the latter
averaging per-class recall; the distinction matters because emotion corpora are
severely imbalanced toward neutral.

**Arousal is easy and valence is hard.** Arousal correlates strongly with
straightforward acoustics — energy, pitch range, speaking rate — so it was
largely solved early. Valence does not: whether an utterance is pleasant or
unpleasant often depends on *what is being said*. This "valence gap" defined the
field for a decade.

The most instructive result here is that transformers closed the gap, and *why*.
Wagner et al. [@wagner2023dawn] fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT variants on
MSP-Podcast and obtained state-of-the-art valence prediction (CCC 0.638) without
any explicit linguistic input. Their analysis of the mechanism is the part worth
teaching: the models succeed **because the transformer layers learn implicit
linguistic information during fine-tuning**, which is why they match multimodal
systems that use transcripts explicitly. The model closed the valence gap by
covertly learning to read.

That finding is a useful corrective in two directions. It explains an apparent
capability without crediting the model with acoustic sensitivity it does not
have, and it connects directly to @sec-modality-gap: a system that appears to
hear emotion may be routing through language, which is the same substitution
that makes audio language models insensitive to pitch.

The same study is unusually careful about robustness and fairness, and reports
a distinction worth carrying: the models were **fair with respect to biological
sex groups but not with respect to individual speakers**. Aggregate group parity
and per-speaker reliability are different properties, and a system can have the
first without the second.

::: {.callout-warning}
## IEMOCAP results are frequently not comparable

IEMOCAP has been the field's default corpus for fifteen years, and papers using
it differ on choices that change results by many points: whether to merge
*excited* into *happy* to reach the conventional four classes, whether to use
improvised or scripted sessions or both, and whether the split is
speaker-independent. A great many reported comparisons are therefore between
different tasks wearing the same name. MSP-Podcast, larger and drawn from
natural speech, is the better modern default.
:::


## Audio Captioning and Language-Aligned Audio {#sec-aac}

**Automated audio captioning** asks for a free-text description of a clip — "a
dog barks twice as a car passes" — which is the general-audio analogue of the
open-ended understanding that audio language models aim at. The standard corpora
are AudioCaps and Clotho [@drossos2020clotho], the latter deliberately
multi-reference, with five captions per clip.

Captioning inherited its metrics from image captioning, and they did not
transfer. Zhou et al. [@zhou2022fense] built human-judgement benchmarks for
audio captions — using pairwise comparisons rather than absolute ratings,
precisely because pairwise judgements achieve better annotator agreement — and
found that SPICE, CIDEr, and SPIDEr [@liu2017spider] correlate *poorly* with
human assessment. Their replacement, **FENSE**, combines Sentence-BERT
similarity with a learned error detector that penalises fluent but incorrect
sentences, and improves agreement with human judgement by 14–25%. The
methodological lesson is the same one @sec-tts-eval reaches from a different
direction: a borrowed metric requires validation in its new domain, and this one
was used for years without it.

### Contrastive Audio-Text Models {#sec-clap}

The other way to connect audio to language is not to generate text but to
**align** the two in a shared embedding space. CLAP [@elizalde2023clap;
@wu2023laionclap] applies the CLIP recipe to audio: an audio encoder $f$ and a
text encoder $g$ trained on paired data with a symmetric contrastive objective
over a batch,

$$
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}
\left[
\log \frac{e^{\,s(a_i, t_i)/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{\,s(a_i, t_j)/\tau}}
+
\log \frac{e^{\,s(a_i, t_i)/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{\,s(a_j, t_i)/\tau}}
\right]
$$ {#eq-clap}

with $s(a,t) = \cos\big(f(a), g(t)\big)$ and temperature $\tau$.

What this buys is **an open label set**. Classification becomes ranking a set of
text prompts against the audio embedding, so the classes need not be fixed at
training time and adding a new one costs nothing. It also gives text-to-audio
retrieval directly, and — as @sec-tts-eval noted for FAD — a general-purpose
audio embedding space that turns out to correlate with human perceptual
judgement better than codec latents do.

CLAP and audio language models are complementary rather than competing. CLAP is
a single forward pass per candidate and is the right tool for retrieval,
tagging, and filtering at scale; a generative model is the right tool when the
answer is a sentence rather than a ranking.


## Other Paralinguistic Inferences {#sec-para-other}

A short catalogue, since these share the machinery above and differ mainly in
what is being inferred and at what risk.

**Speaker traits** — age, sex, accent, native language — are standard
classification over speaker embeddings (@sec-features) or SSL features.
**Speech pathology and health** covers dysarthria, Parkinsonian speech, and a
large and methodologically contested literature on inferring depression and
cognitive decline. **Spoofing and deepfake detection** is the countermeasure
side of @sec-cloning: the ASVspoof series [@wang2024asvspoof5] is the standard
evaluation, and its central finding across editions is that detectors generalise
poorly to attack types they were not trained on — which is why the synthesis
chapter treats passive detection as substantially unsolved.

Two of these have a property the others do not: **the inference is about a
person, and can be made without their knowledge**. That is the subject of
@sec-validity.


## Evaluation {#sec-audio-eval}

| Benchmark | Scope |
|:----------|:------|
| **DCASE** challenges | The organising annual event for detection and classification of acoustic scenes and events; defines the tasks, data, and metrics most of this chapter uses |
| **HEAR** [@turian2022hear] | Holistic evaluation of audio representations: one frozen encoder, many downstream tasks spanning speech, music, and environmental sound |
| **SUPERB** [@yang2021superb] | The speech-side equivalent (@sec-superb), including emotion and speaker tasks |
| **AudioSet** tagging (mAP) | The default general-audio classification benchmark |
| **Clotho / AudioCaps** with **FENSE** | Captioning, with a metric validated against human judgement |
| **MMAU**, **AIR-Bench** (@sec-slm-eval) | The audio-LLM successors, which fold these tasks into open-ended question answering |

: Benchmarks for audio understanding. {#tbl-audio-eval}

HEAR is worth singling out for its design. It freezes the encoder and varies only
a shallow downstream head across a deliberately heterogeneous task set, which
tests generality rather than task-specific tuning — the same protocol as SUPERB,
and it revealed the same thing: no single encoder wins everywhere, and speech
encoders and general-audio encoders have genuinely different strengths. That
result is what forces SALMONN's dual-encoder design (@sec-adapter).


## Validity, Fairness, and Regulation {#sec-validity}

This is the one area in this book where the most important open problem is not
technical.

**Construct validity.** Supervised learning assumes the label denotes something
real and stable. For emotion that assumption is contested within psychology
itself. Barrett et al. [@barrett2019emotion] reviewed the evidence on inferring
emotional state from facial movements and concluded that the mapping is far
weaker and more context-dependent than the "universal expression" model assumes.
Their review concerns faces rather than voice, so it is not direct evidence about
speech — but the argument it makes is structural, about whether a fixed set of
expressions reliably signals a fixed set of internal states, and it applies to
vocal expression for the same reasons. A model can be an excellent predictor of
*annotator labels* while those labels are a poor measure of *what the speaker
felt*, and no amount of accuracy resolves the difference.

**Fairness.** Systems inherit the demographic composition of their training data,
which for paralinguistics is usually unknown and rarely balanced. The
distinction from @sec-ser is the operative one: parity across broad groups does
not imply reliability for individuals, and it is individuals who are affected.

**Regulation.** The EU AI Act prohibits placing on the market or using AI systems
that infer emotions in the **workplace and in education**, outside narrow medical
and safety exceptions, and treats emotion recognition as high-risk in other
contexts. This is one of the few places where a research area in this book has
been directly restricted by law, and the stated rationale is the validity concern
above rather than a general objection to the technology. Anyone building in this
area should read the operative text rather than a summary of it, including this
one.

The practical position I would take is that these systems are defensible for
aggregate, consented, low-stakes uses — retrieval, content description,
accessibility, research on populations — and difficult to defend for individual
consequential decisions about people who did not consent to being measured.


## Open Problems {#sec-para-open}

1. **Labels that reflect uncertainty.** Soft labels are a partial answer.
   Training and evaluation protocols that treat annotator disagreement as signal
   rather than noise are still not standard.
2. **Robustness across corpora.** Cross-corpus emotion recognition degrades
   sharply, which suggests models learn corpus-specific recording and elicitation
   artefacts alongside the target attribute.
3. **Disentangling acoustics from language.** The @sec-ser finding that valence
   performance rests on implicit lexical learning means we do not currently know
   how much genuinely *acoustic* affect recognition is achievable.
4. **Weak supervision without temporal degradation.** @eq-mil-pool produces
   frame-level outputs that nothing supervises; better inductive biases or cheap
   forms of temporal supervision remain open.
5. **Generalisation of spoofing countermeasures** to unseen attacks, which every
   ASVspoof edition has identified and none has closed.
6. **Polyphony and overlap.** Real acoustic scenes contain many simultaneous
   sources; most benchmarks under-represent dense overlap.
7. **Do audio LLMs subsume this?** They are broad and weak; specialised models
   are narrow and strong. Whether the general model eventually dominates, as it
   did in text, is unresolved — and @sec-modality-gap suggests the paralinguistic
   part is exactly where it currently does not.


## Summary

What remains in an audio signal after the words have been removed is the subject
of two research communities that share one problem: their labels are
constructions rather than facts. Annotators disagree irreducibly about emotion
and about how to describe a sound, so majority-vote targets discard real
information, reported accuracies live under a ceiling set by human agreement, and
metrics borrowed from domains with unique correct answers mislead.

The non-speech side was organised by AudioSet and by a progression of backbones —
PANNs, AST, BEATs — whose trajectory recapitulates the rest of the book:
convolutional to transformer, supervised to self-supervised, and finally to
iterative masked prediction over learned discrete targets, which is HuBERT's idea
transplanted to general audio. Its distinctive technical problem is supervision
that is weaker than the required output, addressed by multiple-instance learning
with attention pooling and by semi-supervised consistency training, and evaluated
by a score designed not to move when you change an arbitrary threshold.

The speech side's clearest lesson is a negative one. Transformers closed the
long-standing valence gap in emotion recognition, but the mechanism was implicit
lexical learning rather than acoustic sensitivity — the model learned to read.
That is the same substitution of language for audio diagnosed in
@sec-modality-gap, appearing here in a task where it was measured precisely, and
it should make one cautious about any claim that a model has learned to hear
something when reading would also have sufficed.

Finally, this is the part of the field where the binding constraint is not
architecture or data but whether the quantity being predicted exists as labelled.
That question is unresolved in psychology, and it has now been answered
provisionally in law.
